entry.title: I Built an AI Data Assistant for My PM Team Inside SAP
entry.content:
Here's What Modern PM Work Looks Like 

A significant chunk of my week used to look like this.

Open SAP's internal cloud reporting system, filter by industry, export the table. Open SAC, find the right story, apply the filter again. Switch to the CSAT tab, reconcile customer names that never quite match across systems. Then finally answer the question a colleague asked 45 minutes ago.

It wasn't broken. But it wasn't good enough for the pace we need to move at.

So I built something.

 

What I Built

The Industries PM AI Assistant is a natural-language interface over six live SAP data sources. Any PM on our team can ask a question in plain English and get a synthesized answer in under a minute.

Instead of navigating dashboards, you type:

"Show me deal qualification data for Chemicals. What are the top redirect reasons, and do we have CSAT feedback from those customers?"

The assistant pulls redirect counts, ranks the reasons, surfaces relevant satisfaction feedback, and connects the narrative. It runs as a live web app on SAP BTP.

Data sources it talks to:

  • SAP's internal cloud reporting system: customer adoption, scope item usage, instance counts
  • SAC Analytics Cloud: Deal qualification data (17,000+ rows) via the SAP Analytics Cloud API
  • CSAT / Qualtrics: customer satisfaction feedback, enriched with industry via customer master join
  • Competitive battlecards: market intelligence, on demand

It runs on Claude via SAP BTP AI services. No data leaves SAP infrastructure.

 

Why This Matters

Our team covers 12+ industry verticals. Every week we're trying to answer questions like:

  • Which industries have the highest redirect rates, and why?
  • What are Chemicals customers saying in CSAT?
  • Which scope items have low adoption in Process Industries?
  • Where are we losing deals, and to whom?

Each of those requires pulling from two or three systems that don't share a customer ID, don't use the same industry taxonomy, and certainly don't talk to each other.

The assistant does the joining, the filtering, and the synthesis. The PM just asks.

 

The Part That Surprised Me Most

The most impressive capability isn't the data retrieval. It's the cross-source reasoning.

Real example from testing. I asked:

"Show me CSAT for Chemicals customers."

The problem: CSAT has no industry field. There is no Chemicals column to filter on.

Here's what the assistant did:

  • Flagged the limitation: CSAT rows have no industry tag
  • Proposed a fix: name-match CSAT respondents against the Chemicals deal qualification data customer list
  • Ran a fuzzy join across both datasets despite naming differences
  • When the direct join was thin, used the L3-Area field as a manufacturing proxy to surface more relevant feedback
  • Connected the CSAT complaints to the redirect reasons from earlier in the conversation

That kind of analysis used to take a data analyst an afternoon. The assistant did it in a single query, mid-conversation.

 

What This Looks Like Day to Day

Before: I need redirect data for Chemicals for the QBR. Let me pull the SAC story, filter by industry, export, then cross with CSAT...

After: "Summarize redirect trends for Chemicals and flag any CSAT signals." Done in one query.

Before: Which scope items should I prioritize for Process Industries? Let me check CDO, filter by industry, sort by usage rate...

After: "Which scope items have the lowest activation rate in Process Industries?" Instant answer with a chart.

Before: Spending the first 30 minutes of a customer prep call pulling data.

After: Ask the assistant to brief you. Spend those 30 minutes on strategy instead.

 

The Honest Build Story

This was built by a PM. Not a developer, not a data engineer. A PM with some technical background, an AI coding assistant, and evenings.

The stack:

  • Python and FastAPI backend
  • Playwright for browser automation on JS-rendered SAP data sources
  • SAC SAP Analytics Cloud API: SAP Analytics Cloud's API, which bypasses UI pagination and returns the full dataset server-side
  • Claude API via SAP BTP AI services
  • SAP BTP Cloud Foundry for always-on deployment

The hardest part wasn't the AI. It was the data plumbing. Authentication, session management, hidden pagination in SAP's internal cloud reporting system, JS-rendered tables in SAC. That took the majority of build time.

But it's solved. The app re-authenticates automatically, handles session expiry, detects VPN state, and degrades gracefully when a source is unavailable.

 

What's Next

The current version fetches live data from SAP's internal cloud reporting system and SAC. In December 2026, we're migrating the data layer to SAP Data Products. That means cleaner APIs, better governance, and a more scalable foundation that other teams can replicate.

On the roadmap:

  • Automated weekly PM briefings, generated without any manual trigger
  • Jira integration to surface open influence requests and sprint items in context
  • More data sources as SAP's data product catalog grows

 

Why I'm Writing This

Not to show off a tool.

The point is what it represents. PM work looks different when you treat AI as infrastructure rather than a shortcut. The time that used to go into pulling and reconciling data now goes into analysis, customer conversations, and roadmap decisions.

And the bar to build something like this, for a PM with technical curiosity and the right tools, is lower than most people think.

 

Get Involved

If you're a PM in SAP, the assistant is live on BTP. Reach out and I'll get you access or we can talk of extending the app with the data you need.

If you're building something similar inside SAP, happy to share the approach and what I'd do differently. Drop a comment or connect with me directly.

 

Akshay Kaore is a Product Manager for SAP S/4HANA Cloud ERP Industries, focused on Process Industries and Chemicals. 12 years at SAP across engineering, DevOps, and product. He runs AI enablement for the Industries PM team. This post is part of the AI Product Management series on SAP Community. The views expressed here are my own and do not represent the position of my employer.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.

Sources

  • SAP Architecture Center: Third-Party MCP Server Access to SAP Solutions on BTP
  • SAP News Center: New Agentic Capabilities on SAP BTP Supercharge Developers for What's Next (SAP TechEd 2025, 5 Nov 2025)
  • Claude documentation: Share session output as artifacts
  • Skybuffer: MCP server for SAP ECC and S/4HANA
  • Skybuffer AI documentation: Business AI Scenarios Package
  • Skybuffer AI documentation: MCP Server

entry.title: CAP Agents that collaborates with humans - Announcing `cap-agents-sdm-backend` plugin
entry.content:
In my earlier articles, we explored how CAP agents can remember useful information across conversations and find relevant passages in documents using vector stores. But knowledge work often continues beyond finding an answer.

A project assistant or a manager may need to read last week's report, follow a reporting template, prepare this week's update, and save it where the team can review it. The result needs to become a document people can continue working with.

Enterprise Content Management has been a central piece in enterprises for document collaboration through role-based access control and audited work through versioning.

In this post, I'm introducing @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend: an open-source add-on that lets CAP agents work on content and collaborate with humans via SAP Document Management or any compliant CMIS 1.1 repositories through an unified access layer.

SDM as a filesystem for knowledge work

With CAP v10 and the @cap-js/agents plugin, developers can build Calesi-pattern agents within CAP applications. CAP provides the application framework, while the underlying agent harness coordinates the model and its tools.

Tools such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex offer a useful illustration of this working style. An agent explores folders, reads instructions, finds relevant files, and saves its work. The filesystem gives it a practical way to organise and revisit content.

That pattern is useful for business content too. Imagine a workspace containing the following folder layout:

File content layout for agentic work

 The agent can read the instructions (AGENTS.md), discover how to prepare a report (via Agent Skills), inspect earlier work (previously created files), and write a new document. With this backend, the content lives in SAP Document Management rather than on the application's local disk, accessed as a virtual filesystem.

These file operations do not require a shell or a code-execution tool. Hence, this is a better and a more secured approach. The backend translates them into requests to the document repository via the CMIS 1.1 protocol.

A filesystem view for the agent, with content stored in SAP Document Management

@mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend implements the Deep Agents filesystem backend interface for SAP Document Management via CMIS Browser Binding. It is designed to be used with CAP Node.js 10 or later.

It gives the agent familiar operations to:

  • Browse folders and read files (ls command)
  • Create files, including missing parent folders below its configured workspace. (mkdir and >> operations)
  • Edit text within existing files (>> operation)
  • Find files by path patterns and search for literal text in their contents (grep command)

This is direct file access. This is in stark contrast to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through 'Semantic retrieval' using a vector store.

The CMIS Browser Binding approach also makes compatible CMIS repositories a possible backing store or virtual filesystem, subject to their supported capabilities and connection setup.

The source code is open-source and MIT licensed.

A shared workspace for people and agent collaboration

The most useful part is that the documents remain available with people too.

An agent can prepare a report, a team member (human) can review and revise it, and a later conversation can use the saved report as its starting point. The document becomes a shared work product that remains useful beyond the chat.

Content Management Interoperability Services v1.1 (CMIS) brings the content-management layer. Depending on the repository and configuration, this includes role-based access and document or folder permissions, version history, and the auditing capabilities. SAP's Document Management has in-built access controls and versioning for supported repositories.

Collaboration here means people and agents contributing to content in the same repository, through their respective interfaces i.e. UI for humans, while filesystem interface for agents.

People and agents collaborate together on documents

Example: Project Reporting Assistant

I added a basic reports assistant example in the repository demonstrating this pattern in a CAP application with an embedded SAPUI5 Document Management ReuseUI and an agent chat.

The workspace contains agent instructions, reporting skills, and templates. A user supplies a few updates:

Create this week's project status report for Northstar.

Integration testing is complete.
Environment access is still pending.
Carry forward the open actions from the previous report.

The agent reads the relevant instructions and template, consults the previous report, and saves a new text report in the repository. The user can then open the output report for review.

The example includes project status reports, incident reports, and executive briefings. For instance, an incident report can become the source for a later leadership briefing.

In the demo, instructions (AGENTS.md) and skills (Agent Skills) also live in SAP Document Management. Teams can update that content in the repository and start a new chat to load the revised instructions.

Team begins a conversation with an agent, and collaborates on the content

 Demo of Project Reporting Assistant

Getting started

Install the package in your CAP agent application:

npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend

The SdmBackend backend can automatically use the service-binding flow if having an SDM instance binding or can use a configured Cloud SDK destination. And the configured root folder lets the application expose a selected part of the repository as the agent's workspace.

There is no additional CDS persistence model or cds add step for document storage. The package README explains configuration, and the complete example shows the CAP integration and document UI.

Start with text-based content such as instructions, templates, and reports. Access to a file does not automatically provide native editing of Word documents, spreadsheets, or PDFs. Likewise, prompt instructions asking for confirmation or protecting templates need enforceable application controls when those are business requirements.

With this add-on, a CAP agent can leave behind more than a chat response: a report, a working draft, or an updated document that the team can pick up and continue.

Try the example, adapt the workspace to your use case, and share feedback or issues in the repository.

entry.title: Step Zero Before You Put AI on an SAP S/4HANA Process
entry.content:
The person who always closes the purchasing process goes on vacation. Their replacement has the manual, the user ID and access to S/4HANA. By mid-morning, they have already asked five times how to move forward. None of the answers were in the manual.

Now swap the replacement for a Joule agent or an automated workflow. It won’t ask five times. It will do exactly what the documentation says.

 

 

 

That is the question worth asking before you put AI or automation on a process in SAP S/4HANA: is the process written down, or is it held up by the people who know how to run it?

Today there are three good guides for governing AI in business processes: COSO’s guidance on generative AI, FEI’s framework on internal control over financial reporting, and SAP’s playbook for ERP automation. All three agree on the fundamentals: AI in a process needs controls, and those controls must be testable. SAP’s playbook even asks teams to map decision points and codify business rules. What none of them offers is a way to check whether the process is actually written down, or held up by people.

If it isn’t, something happens that nobody sees: the automation passes its tests, because the tests have the same gap as the documentation.

These four tests help you find out first. Each one runs on what is already in S/4HANA, with no new tools and no budget.

1. The replacement test

Give the process documentation to someone who doesn’t run the process, and ask them to run it end to end in the test system, using only what is written.

Threshold: if they need to ask more than three times, the process is not described. It is held up by a person.

It is the most uncomfortable test and the fastest: half a day. And it leaves no room for interpretation: either the purchase order reaches the invoice with what is written, or it doesn’t.

2. The exception test

Take one month of purchase orders and journal entries, and count how many were resolved outside the normal path. S/4HANA keeps a trail:

  • Purchase orders changed after release: every change is stored in change documents (tables CDHDR and CDPOS, object class EINKBELEG).
  • Purchase orders without a prior requisition or outside a contract, when the procedure says otherwise: on the PO item, the requisition field (EKPO-BANFN) and the contract field (EKPO-KONNR) are empty.
  • Manual journal entries at month-end: filter them by document type (SA in the standard) and separate them from the ones the system posts on its own.

Threshold: if more than one in ten needed a decision that is not in the procedure, the process runs on unwritten judgment.

One clarification: recurring manual entries that are on the closing checklist don’t count. The ones that count are those nobody could explain with the procedure in hand.

Every “it depends” is a rule that exists and was never written down. “If the supplier is new, I ask for approval even when the amount doesn’t require it.” An agent doesn’t know that rule.

Time: one day.

3. The repeated-question test

For one week, log every question to the help desk or to key users about this process, and the transaction or Fiori app where it came up.

Threshold: if the same question shows up twice, the documentation describes something different from what is actually done.

This test doesn’t measure people. It measures the distance between the document and the operation.

Time: one week, alongside normal work.

4. The control test

List the controls in the process and ask, for each one, where it lives:

  • Configured in S/4HANA (automated control): a release strategy or approval workflow, a required field, data the system won’t let you save if it’s missing.
  • Or in a person (manual control): someone who reviews a report and “notices.”

Threshold: if the control depends on someone looking at a report, it won’t survive automation.

Configured controls scale on their own, as long as nobody turns them off or works around them. Controls that depend on a person noticing something odd stop existing when volume goes up and nobody is looking.

Time: one day with the process owner.

What to do with the result

None of the four is a pass or fail for the whole process. What they give you is a map: which part of the process is defined, and which part is held up by people who know.

The defined part is ready to automate in S/4HANA. The rest has to be written down first, and the team bringing the tool can’t do that work. It’s done by the people who know the process.

The thresholds are a starting point, not a standard. Adjust them to the risk: a financial close deserves a stricter bar than an office supplies purchase.

Why it matters more than it seems

FEI’s framework lists performance testing among its control approaches: comparing what the AI produces against what is considered correct. It is the most rigorous approach. And “correct” is built from how the process runs today.

If part of that “how” was never written down, the reference is incomplete from day one. The automation passes the test, because the test has the same gap as the documentation. Nothing fails, no alert goes off, and the lost judgment doesn’t show up on any S/4HANA dashboard.

What this does not mean

It doesn’t mean documenting everything before automating anything. That would be the perfect excuse to never start.

It means the process description stops being one more project deliverable and becomes part of the control system. It changes category and it changes owner: it no longer belongs to the project team. It belongs to the process owner.

 

If you have run any of these tests on a real process in S/4HANA, tell me which one your process failed. In my experience, the second one surprises people the most.

References

  • COSO, Achieving Effective Internal Control Over Generative AI (February 2026).
  • FEI, Committee on Corporate Reporting, AI Framework: Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (June 2026).
  • SAP, ERP Automation at Scale: A Playbook for AI-Enabled Operations (SAP blog).

entry.title: Use SAP AI Core Models in VS Code Chat Without a Copilot Plan
entry.content:
VS Code’s Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) support lets developers use provider backed models in Chat without a Copilot plan. That can be useful when a team already has access to models through SAP AI Core and wants to work with them in VS Code.

There’s a small integration challenge with SAP AI Core service keys: they contain OAuth credentials and service URLs, not a standard model API key you can paste into a generic endpoint form. The client needs to exchange these credentials for an access token, then use that token and the correct resource group to make model requests.

I built SAPilot to handle those steps and make supported SAP AI Core deployments available in the VS Code Chat model picker.

What happens between Connect and Chat

After you enter your service key details, SAPilot stores the client secret in VS Code’s SecretStorage. The client ID, authentication URL, AI Core API URL, and resource group are stored separately as nonsecret connection settings. When SAPilot needs to call SAP AI Core, it requests an OAuth access token using the client credentials flow. The token is cached until shortly before it expires.

The exchange is the part that makes a service key different from a simple API key. This shortened example shows the same basic request SAPilot makes:

let tokenUrl = authUrl;
if (!tokenUrl.endsWith('/oauth/token')) tokenUrl += '/oauth/token';

const response = await fetch(`${tokenUrl}?grant_type=client_credentials`, {
  method: 'POST',
  redirect: 'error',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Basic ${Buffer.from(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`).toString('base64')}`
  }
});

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`SAP sign-in failed: ${response.status}`);
const { access_token: accessToken, expires_in: expiresIn } = await response.json();

For a chat request, SAPilot sends the access token as a bearer token and adds the AI-Resource-Group header. It also discovers running deployments and chooses a compatible request format for each supported chat model. This is why connecting SAP AI Core takes more than entering a base URL and a key.

A small security decision with a practical effect

A design choice was where to persist the values entered during setup. SAPilot uses VS Code’s SecretStorage for the client secret and globalState for the client ID and endpoint details. VS Code documents SecretStorage as encrypted storage for sensitive values, while extension state is intended for ordinary key-value data. Keeping the secret out of ordinary configuration avoids writing it alongside nonsecret settings.

This choice also affects setup: the secret is stored locally through VS Code and is not synced between machines, so you enter it again on another machine. SAPilot never needs a shared credential embedded in the extension; each developer connects using their own service key. Prompts and chat context are sent to the SAP AI Core model selected in Chat, so the model and service key should be chosen according to your organization’s data and access policies.

Why use the Chat Provider API?

VS Code’s Language Model Chat Provider API lets an extension contribute models to the existing picker and handle requests for them. SAPilot registers a provider, looks up deployments available to the connected service key, and returns the supported chat deployments to VS Code. When you select one, the extension translates the chat messages into that model’s request format and streams the response back into Chat.

That provider layer is useful here because SAP AI Core can expose different model families and request formats. SAPilot currently handles supported OpenAI compatible Chat Completions, Claude, Bedrock Converse, Cohere Chat, and Gemini on Vertex AI deployments. Deployments that are not supported chat models, such as embeddings, are left out of the picker.

The result is a familiar workflow: connect once, open Chat, and select an SAP AI Core deployment. You do not need to copy an access token into VS Code or manually add a resource-group header for every request.

Getting started and scope

Install SAPilot in VS Code 1.104 or later, run SAPilot: Connect to SAP AI Core, and enter your service key details. You need permission to use a running chat deployment. Then open Chat and select a model under SAP AI Core.

BYOK makes this chat workflow available without a Copilot plan, but model usage still follows the billing terms of your SAP AI Core account. Some VS Code capabilities, including inline suggestions and semantic search, remain tied to GitHub or Copilot services. Model cost, quality, and speed depend on the deployment, usage, and task.

A takeaway and what’s next

SAPilot shows how VS Code’s BYOK support can connect developers to models their organization already provides through SAP AI Core. BYOK changes which service handles chat requests; model usage still follows your SAP AI Core billing and your organization’s data policies. If you try SAPilot, have a question, or would like to suggest a feature, let me know in the comments. You can also contribute by raising a pull request on GitHub.

  • VS Code Language Model Chat Provider API
  • VS Code extension data storage and SecretStorage
  • SAP AI Core: Use a Service Key
  • SAPilot source code

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Look at where the "Agent" rows sit. They are at the edges of the process: interpreting demand, explaining approvals, investigating exceptions and analyzing spend. The middle of the process, where money and goods actually move, belongs to integration. The three-way match is the interesting one. The match itself is a rule. The moment it fails, though, someone has to work out why, and that is exactly the kind of work an agent is good at.

So the question is not "agent or integration?" It is "which part of this step needs judgment?"

3. Two layers that work together

Once you accept that split, the architecture becomes cleaner. I think of it as two layers with a governed boundary between them.

The intelligence layer is where agents live, whether they are Joule agents, custom agents built on SAP BTP, or third-party agents. They understand the request, choose the right tools, interpret results, investigate exceptions and recommend or explain the next step.

The execution layer is SAP Integration Suite: Cloud Integration, API Management, Event Mesh, B2B and the connectivity into S/4HANA, ECC and third-party systems. It connects, transforms, routes, retries, secures and monitors.

An agent investigating a blocked invoice should never need to know how to reach the ERP, how to build the payload or which destination to use. It should ask for the evidence through an approved tool and spend its effort on explaining the discrepancy. The integration layer handles the rest.

Figure 1. Agents handle intent and reasoning; SAP Integration Suite provides governed access to business capabilities.

4. Why MCP matters here

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives compatible AI applications a standard way to discover and call tools. That sounds modest, but think about the alternative. Without a standard, every agent project discovers, interprets and rebuilds access to the same backends. The SAP deck compared it to a craftsperson. A good craftsperson is productive because trusted tools are already on the bench before the work starts. Agents need the same thing.

For a procurement agent, the bench might hold a handful of tools:

  • get_purchase_order to retrieve permitted PO details
  • check_approval_status to read the current approval state
  • validate_purchase_order to run defined validations
  • submit_for_approval to start an authorized approval workflow

Each tool has a clear purpose, a typed input and output contract, and narrow permissions. The agent picks the tool. The integration layer does the work.

One caution, because I hear this misunderstanding often: MCP standardizes the conversation between an agent and a tool. It does not make the tool secure, it does not check whether the user has authority to approve, and it does not guarantee the call succeeds. Those controls still live in the gateway, the integration logic and the backend.

5. Design tools for agents, not catalogs for agents

A typical SAP landscape has hundreds of APIs, iFlows and RFCs, many of them overlapping. The instinct is to expose all of them to the agent and let it figure things out. In my experience that is the fastest way to get an agent that is slow, expensive and unpredictable. Large tool catalogs make tool selection ambiguous, and oversized responses fill the context window with noise.

A lesson from one of my own programs: we built an AI assistant that answered purchase-order status questions for procurement and finance users, with a Vertex AI agent sitting behind Apigee X and calling into Ariba. Before it, these questions went into an email queue and often took a day to answer. After it, the answer came back in a few seconds. The model was not what made it work. What made it work was that the agent saw one narrow, well-described capability with a clean response, rather than the raw Ariba API surface. Most of the effort went into the API, not the prompt.

The same thinking applies to composition. Suppose an invoice-investigation agent needs invoice details, PO details and goods-receipt data. The naive design gives it three tools and asks it to correlate the responses. The better design composes them behind one business-oriented interface and returns a focused, structured result.

Figure 2. From multiple APIs to one agent-centric composed API.

This is now something SAP explicitly calls out: combining multiple backend APIs and exposing them as optimized MCP endpoints for agent consumption. The benefits are real (fewer tool calls, less correlation logic in the agent, smaller context, clearer ownership), but they are not free. Composition moves work into the integration layer, and its effect on latency and cost depends on data volumes, caching and how well you handle partial failures. Design it like any other API, with the same care.

The goal is not to expose more APIs to agents. It is to expose better business capabilities.

6. API-centric integration and the API artifact

Anyone who has worked on BTP for a while knows the split. Integration logic (routing, mapping, orchestration) lives in an iFlow in Cloud Integration. Exposure, security policies and throttling live in an API proxy in API Management. Two artifacts, two experiences, two places to look when something breaks.

API-centric integration introduces the API artifact, a single design and runtime element that combines the qualities of both: secure and publish, policy enforcement and throttling on one side; message routing, transformation and call orchestration on the other. It runs on the Integration Cell, a single runtime for Cloud Integration and API Management. According to the session, that removes extra hops and the double charging that came from passing a call through both. Monitoring is unified through the message processing log (MPL), with analytics feeding the existing API Management dashboards.

The capabilities that caught my attention as an architect:

  • Discovery of backend services from BTP destinations, the SAP Gateway catalog service for on-premise S/4HANA, and systems registered in the BTP cockpit's System Landscape.
  • API specifications attached as OpenAPI, or generated from natural language. A machine-readable spec is what lets an API be extended as an MCP tool, so this matters more than it looks.
  • Security with credentials scoped to a controlled set of APIs instead of master credentials, binding to XSUAA for token exchange across BTP, and principal propagation to on-premise systems. Validation of tokens from external OIDC issuers was shown as roadmap.
  • Developer Hub as one catalog where application developers subscribe to APIs and agents discover MCP servers, with self-registration for credentials.

On adoption, SAP's own recommendation was refreshingly conservative: consider the API artifact in the Integration Cell for greenfield projects, with no changes to existing deployments. I would put it this way:

  1. New work: design with the API artifact where the runtime and features you need are available.
  2. Stable integrations: leave them alone. A working iFlow that meets its SLA is not technical debt.
  3. Targeted modernization: consolidate when a flow is already being redesigned, or when a capability needs governed exposure to agents.
  4. Automation later: treat AI-assisted migration as something to evaluate once it is a supported capability, not something to plan budgets around today.

I have led enough migrations, from Oracle SOA 11g to 12c, from SOA to SAP BTP and from Boomi to Apigee X, to say this plainly: mass conversions without a business reason rarely pay back. Modernize where the change already touches.

7. Three paths to MCP with the MCP Gateway

This is the part I think matters most for SAP customers. The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite exposes your APIs, integrations and data sources as governed MCP servers. The session described three alternative starting points. They are options, not sequential steps.

Figure 3. Three paths to MCP enablement with SAP Integration Suite.

Path 1: from an API artifact. Expose a deployed API artifact's operations natively as MCP tools. This is the natural route for new API-centric work.

Path 2: from existing API specifications. Bring in specifications from existing API Management deployments or external HTTP endpoints. The technical spec is translated into MCP schema and enriched with natural-language semantics so agents can understand what each tool does.

Path 3: from RFCs. Expose remote-enabled function modules from ECC or S/4HANA. For a lot of customers this is the big one. Many core processes still run on ECC and on BAPIs that have been stable for fifteen years. Rebuilding every one of them as a new REST service before an agent can use it would delay adoption by years. That said, not every RFC should be agent-callable. Pick them deliberately, scope them tightly, and keep the backend authorization checks in place.

Two other points are worth noting. First, SAP Architecture Center now positions the MCP Gateway as the endorsed pathway for external third-party agents and for customer-built agents on BTP to reach SAP systems, with federation of third-party MCP servers on the roadmap. Second, MCP itself is still evolving quickly. If you run self-managed MCP servers, you own the job of tracking the specification and planning upgrades. A managed gateway takes that off your plate, which is a reasonable trade for most enterprise teams.

8. Guardrails are part of the design, not an add-on

In classic integration, it was usually enough to know that application X called API Y. With agents, you need to know which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called, what authorization applied, and whether the business outcome was what everyone expected. Before any agent touches a transactional system, I want to see answers to these:

  • Identity and least privilege. Which agents and users can call which tools? Scoped credentials, not shared master keys.
  • Business authorization. Technical access must never bypass approval limits or segregation of duties. Being able to call submit_for_approval is not the same as being allowed to approve.
  • Input validation. Validate tool inputs against schema and business constraints before anything executes.
  • Traffic management. Rate limits, IP restrictions and payload protection, so a looping agent cannot flood an ECC system.
  • Error semantics. A rejected PO is a business outcome. An unreachable backend is a technical failure. The agent needs to be able to tell the difference.
  • Traceability. Enough logging to reconstruct a tool call end to end during an incident or an audit.
  • Human oversight. High-value or policy-sensitive actions go to a person. Design that path in from day one.

9. Context engineering is an integration concern

There is a common assumption that more context makes an agent smarter. Usually it does the opposite. Twenty overlapping tools and a 4,000-line payload make it harder for the model to choose correctly, and you pay for every token.

What works is focused tool descriptions, explicit input and output schemas, composed responses that contain only what the task needs, and retrieval on demand rather than up front. Notice that almost all of those are decisions made in the integration layer, not in the prompt. How well an agent behaves depends a great deal on what the surrounding architecture lets it see, reach and do.

10. Putting it together: invoice exception management

Here is how I would apply all of this to a scenario most SAP customers will recognize: thousands of supplier invoices a month, most of which match cleanly and a minority that do not.

Routine invoices never see an agent. Integration Suite ingests them, converts formats, runs the deterministic three-way match and posts them according to the rules. There is no reason to pay for reasoning on an invoice that matches.

Exceptions are where the agent comes in. When the match fails on a price variance, a missing goods receipt or a suspected duplicate, the agent calls a composed get_invoice_context tool, compares the evidence, explains the likely cause in plain language and recommends a next step.

Resolution stays controlled. The agent can trigger an authorized action within its limits or route a recommendation to an AP specialist. Either way, the integration layer validates the request and executes it with the normal controls.

Measurement decides whether it was worth it. I would track exception resolution time, the manual intervention rate, integration failure rate, cost per agent invocation and the share of cases resolved within policy. If those numbers do not move, the agent is a nice demo and nothing more.

11. A word on cost

Agent cost is not just tokens. It includes repeated tool calls, orchestration overhead, monitoring, governance and the time people spend investigating odd behavior. Keeping agents off deterministic steps is the single biggest lever. After that: reuse existing iFlows and APIs, keep responses small, compose where it saves calls, and measure consumption next to business outcomes. Edition requirements and AI-unit terms for these capabilities can change, so confirm current details with SAP before you build a business case.

Closing thoughts: orchestration, not universal agentization

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the biggest model. It will be won by the teams that connect models to business processes without giving up the reliability, security and discipline that integration teams have spent years building.

If you are starting this week, here is what I would do:

  1. Take one end-to-end process, such as P2P, and score each step for reasoning value versus execution value.
  2. Pick one exception-heavy step where an agent clearly helps.
  3. Design two or three narrow, composed tools for it. Not twenty.
  4. Expose them through the MCP Gateway using whichever path fits: API artifact, existing spec or RFC.
  5. Put identity, authorization, rate limits and logging in place before go-live, and measure the outcome.

For those of us who have spent our careers in integration, this is good news. The skills that agentic AI needs most (clean contracts, governed access, reliable execution, good observability) are the ones we already have. Our job is not shrinking. It is moving one layer closer to the business.

I would like to hear how others are approaching this. Are you exposing RFCs to agents, or holding back until APIs are cleaner? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: Dispute Resolution for Vendor Invoices: MCP Server App Designed in Hours, Not Developed in Months
entry.content:
From sales orders to supplier invoices

The second business AI app on our SAP ECC system works blocked supplier invoices, and it took one day to build.

In Part 1, Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server, we showed the Sales Representative Release Desk. Sales reps work blocked sales orders before the cancel date, and SAP suggests a decision for each order: release, extend, partial ship or cancel. The desk runs live on SAP ECC through Skybuffer AI, our ontology-based MCP server inside SAP.

This part takes the same approach to finance. The Invoice Dispute Desk resolves supplier invoices that SAP blocked for payment. This time the MCP server had no tools for invoice disputes yet, so the AI agent wrote them in ABAP, registered them in SAP and then built the app on top.

That is the advantage of the ontology approach: our MCP server describes SAP to the AI as business tools, not as OData services. When a use case needs more live SAP data or another action in SAP, the autonomous AI agent adds that tool to the server's registry. So apps like this are designed with the business unit in a workshop, in hours, not developed over weeks or months.

The problem: blocked invoices hold cash and burn discounts

Every blocked invoice is cash the treasury can't plan and, often, a cash discount that lapses while it waits.

Logistics invoice verification blocks a supplier invoice for payment when it doesn't match the purchase order and the goods receipt: a price above the order, more billed than received, goods that never arrived, or a manual hold. Duplicates add to the pile. Clearing each one means switching between MRBR, ME23N, MIGO, the vendor's email thread and a spreadsheet of who promised what.

On our demo system the board opened with seven blocked invoices worth 32,902.24 EUR. Of that, 6,976.00 EUR was in dispute, and 637.16 EUR of cash discount was at risk on six invoices that lose it within five days.

The app: one desk from diagnosis to release

The Invoice Dispute Desk puts every blocked invoice on one board, says what to do next, and lets the clerk do it with one tap and a confirmation.

The board

The board: tiles for cash, disputes and discounts, a stage rail and the worklist

Five tiles show what is at stake: invoices blocked for payment, the amount in dispute, the cash discount at risk, cases waiting on vendors, and invoices ready to release. A stage rail moves each invoice from New to Vendor contacted, Waiting, Ready to release and Done. Filters such as "Discount ≤ 5 days" put the money first.

Each row states the issue in plain words ("Wood Glue: 18.90 vs PO 18.00"), the days left for the cash discount, the case status and SAP's suggestion.

Diagnosis and a suggested next step

An invoice with SAP's suggestion and the three-way match per line

Opening an invoice shows the three-way match per line: ordered, received and billed quantity, PO price against billed price, and the amount over the order. A rules engine picks one next step and explains it with the amounts: release, request a credit memo, accept the price, post the goods receipt, reverse a duplicate or investigate.

For Halvorsen's wood glue it found a newer purchase order at the billed price, so it suggests accepting the price rather than fighting it.

Proof one tap away

Drill-down from the invoice into the purchase order and the prices on other orders

Every purchase order, goods receipt, invoice, vendor and material number is a link that opens live SAP data inside the drawer. Tapping the order shows three newer Halvorsen orders at 18.90 EUR, so the price change is visible before anyone accepts it.

Act, with a confirmation

Each action opens a short form and posts nothing until the clerk reviews and confirms:

  • release the payment block, as MRBR does
  • reverse the invoice, as MR8M does
  • accept the billed price: the PO price changes, then the invoice is released
  • post the vendor's credit memo or the goods receipt

A drafted vendor email, sent from SAP and recorded on the case

For a real dispute, the desk drafts the vendor email from a template per dispute type. It sends the email from SAP and moves the case to Vendor contacted, with a follow-up in three days.

Every step on record

The dispute case with owner and follow-up date, and its audit trail

Each disputed invoice gets a case in SAP with a reason, an owner, a follow-up date and an append-only audit trail of who did what. Resolved invoices move to Done, so the team sees what is left and what was settled.

How it was built in one day

Nobody opened a development project. The desk came out of one conversation between me and an AI assistant (Claude), connected to our SAP ECC system through Skybuffer AI.

One MCP server inside SAP builds the tools and runs the app

The assistant builds through the development tools, and the desk runs on the business tools they produce, both through the same server inside SAP.

Skybuffer AI also follows the SAP-endorsed architecture for AI agents: the same MCP server can be consumed through the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite on SAP BTP. That brings SAP's governance layer for AI agents on top, with authentication, rate limiting and observability.

The brief fit in a few lines: build a dispute resolution desk for vendor invoices in SAP ERD. Be creative: create ABAP classes and register them as tools where needed, refresh the MCP server, and create or clean the master and transaction data the demo needs.

From there Claude took over as my autonomous AI development agent, empowered by Skybuffer AI tools. ABAP Code Intelligence, one of those tools, guarded code integrity, so the new ABAP fits our existing code. The agent worked through SAP the way a developer would, only faster:

  1. Explore. It read the framework conventions and the existing tools in the MCP server, then the invoice landscape: RBKP, RSEG, EKBE and the blocked-invoice table RBKP_BLOCKED.
  2. Design. It proposed the toolset and the data model: a dispute case table, an audit trail table and a rules engine for the three-way match.
  3. Build. It created the tables and the ABAP classes through the MCP server's development tools, activated them and recorded them in a workbench transport.
  4. Register. It registered each class as an MCP tool, in a customizing transport, and refreshed the MCP server.
  5. Test live. It created four demo vendors with .example mailboxes, purchase orders, goods receipts and invoices, and tested every tool against them in SAP.
  6. Build the app. It built the desk on top of the tools and tested it end to end.

I reviewed the plan and the results. Every generated ABAP file header says so: requirements and review by me, design and implementation by Claude.

What the AI generated in SAP

The assistant generated nine MCP tools in ABAP, a rules engine and two tables.

X-ray of the desk: which generated tool sits behind each part of the screen

MCP tool What it does Writes to SAP

get_disputed_vendor_invoicesThe worklist: blocked invoices, open cases, totals and discount at riskno
get_vendor_invoice_dispute_detailOne invoice: three-way match per line, suggestion, case and audit trailno
manage_vendor_invoice_disputeOpens, updates, annotates and closes a dispute casecase tables only
post_vendor_invoicePosts an invoice or the vendor's credit memo, linked to the disputed invoicean invoice document, as MIRO
accept_invoice_priceChanges the PO price to the billed price, through BAPI_PO_CHANGEPO net price
release_blocked_vendor_invoiceRemoves the payment block, optionally moving the baseline date to keep the discountpayment block
reverse_vendor_invoiceReverses a duplicate or wrong invoice, through BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CANCELa reversal document
get_purchase_order_historyA PO with its history, its invoices and the prices of the same material on other ordersno
get_material_documentA goods receipt with quantities, values and reversalsno

Behind the tools sit the rules engine class /SKYBFR/CL_YAI_VIDSP, the case table /SKYBFR/YAIVIDC and the audit trail table /SKYBFR/YAIVIDL. The engine holds the three-way match, the rules and the open posting period. Both tables are also published as data sources, so the assistant can answer questions such as "which vendors take longest to reply?"

The desk also reuses tools the server already had: send_email, post_goods_receipt, get_vendor_details and get_material_stock. Everything sits in a workbench transport and a customizing transport, which go through normal change management.

Same pattern, second process

Both desks follow one pattern: a worklist of what SAP blocked, a diagnosis with a suggested decision, one-tap actions behind a confirmation, and a record of who did what. Only the business content changes.

  Sales Representative Release Desk (Part 1) Invoice Dispute Desk (Part 2)

ProcessSales orders on a delivery blockSupplier invoices blocked for payment
Who works itSales repsAccounts payable clerks
Deadline on screenThe order's cancel dateThe cash discount date
SAP suggestsRelease, extend, partial ship or cancel, from the ATP check and inbound receiptsRelease, credit memo, accept price, goods receipt, reverse or investigate, from the three-way match
Stages8 steps, from identify to follow upNew, vendor contacted, waiting, ready to release, done
Changes in SAPSales order changes through change_sales_orderRelease, reversal, PO price, credit memo, goods receipt, case log
Contact notes keptIn the page's shared storeIn SAP tables, with an audit trail
Partner emailDrafted for the rep to sendSent from SAP
MCP tools used713: 9 generated, 4 reused

The difference that matters: the Sales Representative Release Desk ran on tools the MCP server already had. The Invoice Dispute Desk needed new ones, and the AI built them in the same day.

Security and governance

The desk changes SAP only through tools that check the user's SAP authorizations, and only after the user confirms.

  • SAP authorizations apply. Each tool checks the authorizations of the person using it: M_RECH_BUK for invoice verification, M_BEST_EKO and M_BEST_EKG for purchase orders, M_MSEG_WMB for goods movements. With a direct connection, people sign in to the MCP server with their own SAP user through single sign-on.
  • Nothing posts without a confirmation. Every write opens a form and waits for Review and confirm. Postings go through standard SAP logic, such as BAPI_PO_CHANGE and BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CANCEL.
  • The page calls only what it declares. The desk lists the SAP tools it may use, and Claude asks each user before the first call.
  • No copy of SAP data. The desk reads live from SAP each time it opens. Cases and the audit trail are SAP tables.
  • Normal change management. Generated objects travel in transports, so they are reviewed and moved through the landscape like any other development.
  • Any model. Skybuffer AI works with Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or a self-hosted model. We built this desk with Claude.

What's next

Two processes, two desks, one MCP server: the next business app is a conversation away, and it can bring its own ABAP tools with it.

The 3-minute video shows the Invoice Dispute Desk on a phone, from the blocked board to the x-ray of the generated tools.

Which process should we take on next? Tell us in the comments. Questions about the ABAP side, the rules engine or the MCP server are welcome there too.
